note: Areas show ground the Mongols had conquered or overrun (and, for Western Xia in 1226–27, Hungary and Poland in 1241, ground the base map misdraws); moving circles mark armies on campaign, not conquests. Lines are approximate reconstructions from campaign maps and the chronicles.

chapters.title: Western Xia submits
arrows: Genghis Khan invades Western Xia (spring 1209)
The Mongols push up the Yellow River to Zhongxing (summer–autumn 1209)
chapters.text: Genghis Khan's first big attack on a settled kingdom fell on the Tangut state of Western Xia, which guarded the road from the steppe into China. In 1209 his army beat a Tangut force outside Wulahai, took the town and pushed through the Helan mountains to the capital Zhongxing (Yinchuan). The city held out for months, even when the Mongols tried to flood it, but in January 1210 Emperor Xiangzong submitted and became a vassal paying tribute.

chapters.title: Into Jin China
arrows: Genghis Khan crosses the Jin frontier to Yehuling (1211)
The Mongols break through the Juyong pass to Zhongdu (1213)
The Mongols return to blockade Zhongdu (1214–1215)
chapters.text: In 1211 Genghis invaded the Jurchen Jin empire of northern China and routed its army in the passes of Yehuling. Without siege skills the Mongols at first could only plunder the countryside, but by November 1213 they had forced the Juyong pass and reached the walls of the capital Zhongdu (Beijing). The Jin bought a truce in 1214 and moved their court south to Kaifeng; the Mongols came back, and in June 1215 starving Zhongdu surrendered and was sacked. The Mongols now held the north of the Jin empire.

chapters.title: Qara Khitai
arrows: Jebe rides west against Kuchlug (1218)
Jebe pursues Kuchlug to Kashgar and Badakhshan (1218)
chapters.text: Kuchlug, a Naiman prince who had fled the Mongols, had seized the Central Asian empire of Qara Khitai and persecuted its Muslims. Genghis sent his general Jebe after him, and Jebe won over the towns by promising freedom of worship. In 1218 Kuchlug fled south and was caught and beheaded in Badakhshan. Qara Khitai's lands, from Balasagun to Kashgar and Khotan, passed to the Mongols, who now bordered the Khwarazmian Empire.

chapters.title: Otrar, Bukhara and Samarkand
arrows: Genghis Khan's army marches to Otrar (autumn 1219)
Genghis crosses the Kyzylkum desert to Bukhara (February 1220)
Genghis marches from Bukhara to Samarkand (March 1220)
chapters.text: After the governor of Otrar killed the merchants of a Mongol caravan in 1218, Genghis invaded the Khwarazmian Empire in 1219. While his sons besieged Otrar, he crossed the Kyzylkum desert and appeared at Bukhara, which surrendered on 10 February 1220. Otrar fell the same month, and Samarkand's garrison gave up on 16 March. Shah Muhammad II, who had spread his troops among the cities, fled west, and by the end of the year the Mongols held the land between the Syr Darya and the Amu Darya.

chapters.title: Jebe and Subutai's great ride
arrows: Jebe and Subutai ride into the Caucasus (1220–1221)
Jebe and Subutai cross the Caucasus to the steppe (1222)
Jebe and Subutai turn back to the Kalka (May 1223)
chapters.text: Jebe and Subutai, sent with about 20,000 horsemen to hunt the fleeing shah, did not turn back when he died on a Caspian island in December 1220. They rode into the Caucasus, routed a Georgian army at Khunan, crossed the mountains and defeated the Alans and the Cumans of the steppe. The Cumans called on the Rus' princes, whose armies the Mongols lured into a long pursuit and destroyed on the Kalka river on 31 May 1223. Then they rode back east.

chapters.title: The destruction of Khwarazm and Khorasan
arrows: Genghis's sons march down the Amu Darya to Gurganj (1220–1221)
Tolui marches on Merv and Nishapur (spring 1221)
Genghis marches south against Jalal al-Din (autumn 1221)
chapters.text: In 1221 the Mongols destroyed the cities of the Khwarazmian heartland and Khorasan. Gurganj, the old capital, fell in April after a long siege, and Genghis's son Tolui took Merv and Nishapur and killed most of their people. The shah's son Jalal al-Din raised a new army near Ghazni and beat a Mongol force at Parwan, but Genghis caught him on the Indus on 24 November 1221. Jalal al-Din escaped across the river, and the Khwarazmian Empire was finished.

chapters.title: The end of Western Xia
arrows: Genghis Khan invades the Hexi corridor (1226)
The Mongols march on Lingzhou and Zhongxing (winter 1226–1227)
chapters.text: Western Xia had refused to send troops against Khwarazm and then allied with the Jin, so in 1226 Genghis invaded again. His armies took the cities of the Hexi corridor, Suzhou, Ganzhou and Wuwei, destroyed the Tangut army near the Yellow River in the winter and in 1227 besieged the capital Zhongxing. Genghis died in August 1227, but his death was kept secret, and in September the last Tangut ruler surrendered and was executed. Western Xia ceased to exist.

chapters.title: The fall of the Jin
arrows: Tolui's march through Song territory (1231–1232)
Ögedei crosses the Yellow River (January 1232)
Subutai advances to Kaifeng (April 1232)
Mongol army marches on Caizhou (late 1233)
chapters.text: By 1230 the Jin held little more than Henan and the Wei valley, guarded by the Yellow River and the Tong pass. Ögedei took Fengxiang in 1231 and then sent Tolui on a long march round the Jin defences through Song territory; on 9 February 1232 Tolui destroyed the last Jin field army at Sanfengshan. Subutai besieged Kaifeng, which surrendered on 29 May 1233, and the last Jin emperor fled to Caizhou. Mongol and Song armies stormed it on 9 February 1234, and the Jin dynasty ended.

chapters.title: The conquest of Rus'
arrows: Batu's army attacks Ryazan (December 1237)
The Mongols march on Vladimir (January–February 1238)
Mongol columns sweep north to the Sit and Torzhok (February–March 1238)
The Mongols take Pereyaslavl and Chernigov (1239)
Batu crosses the Dnieper to Kiev (November 1240)
chapters.text: In winter 1237, using the frozen rivers as roads, Batu and Subutai led the western campaign into the Rus' principalities. They stormed Ryazan on 21 December, took Vladimir on 8 February 1238, ravaged fourteen towns of the north-east and killed Grand Prince Yuri II at the Sit river in March, before the thaw stopped them short of Novgorod. In 1239 they sacked Pereyaslavl and Chernigov, and on 6 December 1240 they stormed Kiev.

chapters.title: Poland and Hungary
arrows: The main Mongol army crosses the Verecke pass (March 1241)
Batu advances to the Sajó at Mohi (April 1241)
The Mongols cross the frozen Danube (winter 1241–1242)
chapters.text: In 1241 the Mongols struck central Europe. A diversionary force sacked Sandomierz and Kraków and on 9 April destroyed Duke Henry II's army at Legnica, while the main army crossed the Carpathians and on 11 April annihilated King Béla IV's army at Mohi. The Mongols held the Hungarian plain through 1241, crossed the frozen Danube at Christmas and chased Béla to the Dalmatian coast. In March 1242, after news of Great Khan Ögedei's death, they withdrew.

chapters.title: The Assassins and Baghdad
arrows: Hulagu marches on the Assassin castles (autumn 1256)
Baiju's column crosses the Tigris west of Baghdad (January 1258)
Hulagu's main army advances on Baghdad from the east (January 1258)
chapters.text: Great Khan Möngke sent his brother Hulagu west to subdue Iran and the caliphate. In November 1256 the Nizari Ismaili imam surrendered, and Alamut and the other Assassin castles were given up and destroyed. Caliph al-Musta'sim refused to submit, so in January 1258 Mongol armies closed on Baghdad from both banks of the Tigris. The city surrendered on 10 February and was sacked, and the caliph was executed: the Abbasid caliphate of Baghdad was ended.

chapters.title: Syria and Ain Jalut
arrows: Hulagu crosses the Euphrates to Aleppo (January 1260)
Kitbuqa marches on Damascus (February 1260)
Mongol raiders ride south to Gaza (spring 1260)
Qutuz and Baybars march out of Egypt (July 1260)
The Mamluks advance to Ain Jalut (August–September 1260)
chapters.text: In January 1260 Hulagu crossed the Euphrates, stormed Aleppo and massacred its people; Damascus surrendered on 1 March, and Mongol raiders reached Gaza. Then news of Möngke's death led Hulagu to withdraw most of his army, leaving Kitbuqa with perhaps 10,000–20,000 men. The Mamluk sultan Qutuz marched out of Egypt, retook Gaza and on 3 September 1260 defeated and killed Kitbuqa at Ain Jalut. Within days the Mamluks entered Damascus, and the Mongol advance in the west was over.

battles.name: Siege of Zhongxing
battles.casualties: Unknown; the siege ended in a negotiated submission

battles.name: Battle of Yehuling
battles.casualties: Jin losses described as devastating, Mongol losses light; no reliable figures

battles.name: Sieges of Zhongdu
battles.casualties: Very heavy: famine and disease in the city, thousands massacred after the surrender

battles.name: Siege of Otrar
battles.casualties: Garrison of 5,000–15,000 almost entirely killed; Mongol losses minimal

battles.name: Siege of Bukhara
battles.casualties: Most of the garrison of 2,000–20,000 killed

battles.name: Siege of Samarkand
battles.casualties: Heavy; contemporary figures of hundreds of thousands are exaggerated

battles.name: Battle of Khunan
battles.casualties: Heavy Georgian and Armenian losses from an army of about 10,000

battles.name: Battle of the Kalka River
battles.casualties: Rus' and Cuman losses heavy (most of an army of 20,000–45,000); Mongol losses light

battles.name: Siege of Gurganj
battles.casualties: Very heavy; most of the population killed or enslaved

battles.name: Siege of Merv
battles.casualties: Most of the population killed; chroniclers' 700,000–1,300,000 is a gross exaggeration

battles.name: Siege of Nishapur
battles.casualties: City destroyed and most of its people killed; chroniclers' figures exaggerated

battles.name: Battle of Parwan
battles.casualties: Heavy Mongol losses from a force of about 30,000

battles.name: Battle of the Indus
battles.casualties: Almost all of Jalal al-Din's army of about 30,000 killed

battles.name: Siege of Zhongxing (1227)
battles.casualties: Very heavy; much of the population massacred after the surrender

battles.name: Battle of Sanfengshan
battles.casualties: Jin army of about 150,000 largely destroyed; Mongol losses heavy

battles.name: Siege of Kaifeng
battles.casualties: Very heavy: much of the defending army and of the city's people died, many from plague and famine

battles.name: Siege of Caizhou
battles.casualties: Heavy; the Jin garrison was destroyed and the last two emperors died

battles.name: Siege of Ryazan
battles.casualties: City stormed and most of its people killed

battles.name: Siege of Vladimir
battles.casualties: Defenders and the grand prince's family killed; survivors enslaved

battles.name: Battle of the Sit River
battles.casualties: Army of Vladimir-Suzdal destroyed and Grand Prince Yuri II killed

battles.name: Siege of Kozelsk
battles.casualties: Town destroyed; the Mongols reportedly lost 4,000 men

battles.name: Siege of Kiev
battles.casualties: Defenders and many inhabitants killed (one estimate about 48,000 including civilians)

battles.name: Battle of Legnica
battles.casualties: Polish army of 2,000–8,000 largely destroyed and Duke Henry II killed

battles.name: Battle of Mohi
battles.casualties: Most of the Hungarian army killed (about 10,000 by contemporary accounts); Mongol losses lighter

battles.name: Siege of Alamut
battles.casualties: Light; the castles surrendered

battles.name: Siege of Baghdad
battles.casualties: Very heavy: tens of thousands at least (200,000 by Hulagu's claim; Muslim sources far higher)

battles.name: Siege of Aleppo
battles.casualties: Heavy; nearly all adult men massacred over six days

battles.name: Battle of Ain Jalut
battles.casualties: Heavy Mongol losses from an army of 10,000–20,000, Kitbuqa killed; Mamluk losses unknown
